description: Warnings: the program compiles, but the compiler's analysis found code that is very likely a bug.

rules.title: = used instead of == in a condition
patterns: ^suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value$
^using the result of an assignment as a condition without parentheses$
rules.what: The condition on line {line} uses `=` (assignment) instead of `==` (comparison). `if (x = 5)` STORES 5 in x and is then always true.
why: In maths `=` means 'equals'; in C/C++ `=` means 'store' and `==` means 'is equal to'.
fix: Use `==` to compare: `if (x == 5)`.
rules.tip: Some programmers write constants first, `if (5 == x)`, so that a typo `5 = x` becomes a compile error.
samples: suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value
using the result of an assignment as a condition without parentheses

rules.title: Variable used before it has a value
patterns: ^'(?P<name>[^']+)' is used uninitialized(?: in this function)?$
^'(?P<name>[^']+)' may be used uninitialized(?: in this function)?$
^variable '(?P<name>[^']+)' (?:is|may be) uninitialized when used (?:here|within its own initialization)$
rules.what: `{name}` is read on line {line} before any value was stored in it. Local variables in C/C++ start with GARBAGE (a random leftover value), not 0.
why: The variable was declared without `= 0` (or another starting value), e.g. a sum or counter.
scanf was given the variable without `&`, so it never received the input.
fix: Give it a starting value where it is declared: `int {name} = 0;`.
samples: 'x' is used uninitialized
variable 'sum' is uninitialized when used here
'x' may be used uninitialized

rules.title: Variable declared but never used
rules.what: `{name}` is created but never used afterwards.
why: Leftover code, or you used a different (misspelled) name where you meant `{name}`.
fix: Delete the variable if it is not needed, or use it where intended.
samples: unused variable 'x'
variable 'p' set but not used

rules.title: Function may end without returning a value
patterns: ^non-void function does not return a value(?: in all control paths)?$
^no return statement in function returning non-void$
^control may reach end of non-void function$
rules.what: Function `{func}` promises to return a `{rtype}`, but some path through it reaches the closing `}` without a `return` statement. The caller then receives garbage.
why: An if / else-if chain returns in every branch you thought of, but not in the remaining case (e.g. x == 0).
The final `return` was forgotten.
fix: Add a `return` statement before the closing `}` on line {line} that covers the remaining case.
samples: control reaches end of non-void function
non-void function does not return a value in all control paths

rules.title: Returning the address of a local variable
patterns: ^address of stack memory associated with (?:local variable|parameter) '(?P<name>[^']+)' returned$
rules.what: The function returns the address of a local variable. Local variables are destroyed when the function ends, so the returned pointer points to memory that is no longer valid.
why: Returning `&x` or a local array from a function.
fix: Return the value itself instead of its address, use `static`, or allocate with `malloc` (and free it later).
samples: function returns address of local variable
address of stack memory associated with local variable 'x' returned

rules.title: printf/scanf format does not match the variable
patterns: ^format '(?P<spec>%[^']*)' expects argument of type '(?P<expected>[^']+)', but argument (?P<argn>\d+) has type '(?P<actual>[^']+)'(?: \{aka '(?P<aka>[^']+)'\})?$
^format specifies type '(?P<expected>[^']+)' but the argument has (?:underlying )?type '(?P<actual>[^']+)'$
rules.what: In the {func} call on line {line}, the placeholder `{spec}` expects a `{expected}`, but the value given is a `{actual}`.
why: The wrong % code for the variable's type.
`&` missing in scanf (scanf needs the ADDRESS of the variable).
fix: Use the matching placeholder: %d int, %f float/double (printf), %lf double (scanf), %c char, %s string.
rules.tip: Wrong format codes do not stop compilation, but they print garbage or even crash the program at run time.
samples: format '%d' expects argument of type 'int *', but argument 2 has type 'int'
format specifies type 'int' but the argument has type 'double'

rules.title: Fewer values than % placeholders
rules.what: The format string on line {line} has more `%` placeholders than values after it, so printf/scanf will read garbage for the missing ones.
why: A variable was forgotten after the format string.
fix: Give one value for every `%` code, in the same order.
samples: format '%d' expects a matching 'int' argument
more '%' conversions than data arguments

rules.title: Extra values not used by the format
patterns: ^data argument not used by format string$
rules.what: The printf/scanf call on line {line} passes more values than there are `%` placeholders, so the extra values are ignored.
why: The `%d` (or other code) for a value was forgotten in the format string.
fix: Add a placeholder for every value, e.g. `printf("Value %d\n", x);`.
samples: too many arguments for format
data argument not used by format string

rules.title: Strings compared with ==
patterns: ^comparison with string literal results in unspecified behavio(?:u)?r$
^result of comparison against a string literal is unspecified.*$
rules.what: `==` on line {line} compares the ADDRESSES of two strings, not their text, so it is almost never true.
why: In C, strings are char arrays; `==` checks whether they are the same memory, not the same letters.
fix: Use `strcmp(a, b) == 0` (from `<string.h>`) to compare text.
samples: comparison with string literal results in unspecified behavior
result of comparison against a string literal is unspecified (use an explicit string comparison function instead)
comparison between two arrays
array comparison always evaluates to false

rules.title: Comparing a pointer (or string) with a number / char
patterns: ^ISO C\+\+ forbids comparison between pointer and integer$
rules.what: Line {line} compares a pointer/string with a number or a single character, which is never what you want.
why: Double quotes `"y"` (a string) were used where single quotes `'y'` (a character) were meant.
fix: Compare characters with single quotes: `if (c == 'y')`.
samples: comparison between pointer and integer
comparison between pointer and integer ('char' and 'char *')

rules.title: Indentation suggests braces that are not there
patterns: ^misleading indentation; statement is not part of the previous '(?P<kw>\w+)'$
rules.what: Without `{ }`, only ONE statement belongs to the `{kw}`. The next line is indented as if it were inside, but it always runs.
why: Braces were left out because the body started as one line and a second line was added later.
A `;` right after the condition made the body empty.
fix: Put the statements that belong to the `{kw}` inside `{ }`.
samples: this 'if' clause does not guard...
misleading indentation; statement is not part of the previous 'if'

rules.title: Semicolon makes the if/loop body empty
patterns: ^suggest braces around empty body in an? '(?P<kw>if|else|do)' statement$
rules.what: The `;` right after `{kw} (...)` on line {line} is a complete (empty) statement, so the code below it is NOT controlled by the `{kw}`.
why: A habit of ending every line with `;` - but `if (...)`, `for (...)` and `while (...)` lines must not end with one.
fix: Remove the `;` after the closing `)`.
samples: if statement has empty body
while loop has empty body

rules.title: Statement that does nothing
patterns: ^(?:left|right)-hand operand of comma expression has no effect$
^left operand of comma operator has no effect$
rules.what: The statement on line {line} calculates something but the result is thrown away, so it has no effect.
why: `==` written where `=` was meant (`x == 5;`).
A calculation without storing it (`i + 1;` instead of `i = i + 1;`).
Commas instead of semicolons in a for loop.
fix: Store the result (`x = 5;`, `i = i + 1;`) or remove the statement.
samples: statement with no effect
equality comparison result unused

rules.title: Division by zero
rules.what: Line {line} divides by the constant 0. Integer division by zero crashes the program ("Floating point exception").
why: A typo, or a placeholder value left in the code.
fix: Divide by the intended non-zero value, or check the divisor with `if (d != 0)` first.
samples: division by zero
division by zero is undefined

rules.title: Array index outside the array
patterns: ^array index (?P<index>-?\d+) is (?:past the end of|before the beginning of) the array.*$
rules.what: Line {line} accesses an element outside the array. An array of size N has valid indexes 0 to N-1 only.
why: Using index N (e.g. `a[5]` for `int a[5]`) - the last element is `a[4]`.
A loop condition `i <= N` that runs one step too far.
fix: Use indexes 0 to N-1, and loop with `i < N`.
samples: array index 5 is past the end of the array (that has type 'int[5]')
array subscript 5 is above array bounds of 'int[5]'

rules.title: switch case falls through
rules.what: A `case` block on line {line} has no `break`, so execution continues into the next case.
why: The `break;` at the end of the case was forgotten.
fix: End each case with `break;` (unless falling through is really intended).

example.right:
case 1: printf("one"); break;
case 2: printf("two"); break;

samples: this statement may fall through

rules.title: Function name used without calling it
patterns: ^the address of '(?P<name>[^']+)' will always evaluate as 'true'$
^the comparison will always evaluate as '(?P<value>true|false)' for the address of '(?P<name>[^']+)' will never be NULL$
rules.what: `{name}` is used in a condition without `( )`, so you are testing the function's ADDRESS (always non-zero = true) instead of calling it.
why: Forgetting the brackets and arguments of a function call: `if (isEven)` instead of `if (isEven(n))`.
fix: Call the function: `{name}(...)` with its arguments.
samples: the address of 'isEven' will always evaluate as 'true'
address of function 'isEven' will always evaluate to 'true'

rules.title: Value changes when converted
patterns: ^overflow in conversion from '(?P<from>[^']+)' to '(?P<to>[^']+)' changes value from '(?P<v1>.+?)' to '(?P<v2>.+?)'$
^(?:implicit )?conversion from '(?P<from>[^']+)' to '(?P<to>[^']+)' changes value from '?(?P<v1>[^']+?)'? to '?(?P<v2>[^']+?)'?$
^large integer implicitly truncated to unsigned type$
rules.what: On line {line} a value is stored in a type that is too small (or too different) for it, so the value is silently changed.
why: Storing several characters or a big number in a `char`, or a decimal number in an `int`.
fix: Use a type big enough for the value (`int`, `long long`, `double`) or the right literal.
samples: overflow in conversion from 'int' to 'char' changes value from '24930' to '98'
implicit conversion from 'int' to 'char' changes value from 24930 to 98

rules.title: Comparing signed and unsigned numbers
patterns: ^comparison of integer expressions of different signedness: '(?P<t1>[^']+)'(?: \{aka '[^']+'\})? and '(?P<t2>[^']+)'(?: \{aka '[^']+'\})?$
^comparison of integers of different signs: '(?P<t1>[^']+)' and '(?P<t2>[^']+)'$
rules.what: Line {line} compares a signed number (`{t1}`) with an unsigned one (`{t2}`). If the signed value is negative, the comparison gives the wrong answer.
why: Looping `for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); i++)` - `size()` is unsigned.
fix: Use the same type on both sides, e.g. `size_t i` or `(int)v.size()`.
samples: comparison of integer expressions of different signedness: 'int' and 'std::vector<int>::size_type' {aka 'long unsigned int'}

rules.title: printf with a variable as the format string
patterns: ^format not a string literal and no format arguments$
^format string is not a string literal.*$
rules.what: The first argument of printf on line {line} is not a string in double quotes. If the text contains a `%`, printf will misbehave.
why: `printf(name)` instead of `printf("%s", name)`.
Single quotes used for text: `printf('Hello')`.
fix: Write `printf("%s", text);` - or put the text directly in double quotes.
samples: format not a string literal and no format arguments
format string is not a string literal (potentially insecure)

rules.title: Operator precedence trap
patterns: ^comparisons like '(?P<expr>.+)' do not have their mathematical meaning$
^comparison of constant '(?P<c>[^']+)' with boolean expression is always (?P<value>true|false)$
^result of comparison of constant (?P<c>\S+) with (?:expression of type 'bool'|boolean expression) is always (?P<value>true|false)$
^logical not is only applied to the left hand side of (?:this )?comparison$
rules.what: The expression on line {line} is not grouped the way it reads. C/C++ applies operators in a fixed order (precedence), which differs from maths here.
why: `0 < x < 10` is evaluated as `(0 < x) < 10`, which is always true.
`x & 1 == 0` is evaluated as `x & (1 == 0)`.
`!x == 5` is evaluated as `(!x) == 5`.
fix: Write the condition explicitly: `0 < x && x < 10`, or add brackets: `(x & 1) == 0`.
samples: comparisons like 'X<=Y<=Z' do not have their mathematical meaning
suggest parentheses around comparison in operand of '&'

rules.title: Return value of scanf ignored
rules.what: `{func}` returns a result that tells you whether it worked, but the program ignores it.
why: scanf returns how many values it read; if the user typed letters instead of a number it returns 0 and the variable keeps garbage.
fix: Check it: `if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1) { /* invalid input */ }` - or ignore this warning in simple lab programs.
samples: ignoring return value of 'scanf' declared with attribute 'warn_unused_result'

rules.title: char used as an array index
rules.what: A `char` is used as an array index on line {line}. On some systems char can be negative, giving a negative index.
why: Indexing a counting array with a character, e.g. `count[ch]`.
fix: Convert it: `count[(unsigned char)ch]`, or use an int index.
samples: array subscript has type 'char'

rules.title: Function declared without a parameter list
patterns: ^a function declaration without a prototype is deprecated.*$
^passing arguments to '(?P<name>\w+)' without a prototype is deprecated.*$
rules.what: A function is declared with empty brackets `()` or in an old style. In C, empty brackets mean 'unknown parameters', so the compiler cannot check the calls.
why: Writing `int f()` instead of `int f(void)` in C, or a line that the compiler had to treat as an old-style declaration because of an earlier mistake.
fix: Write `(void)` for functions without parameters, or list the parameters with their types.
samples: a function declaration without a prototype is deprecated in all versions of C and is treated as a zero-parameter prototype in C23, conflicting with a previous declaration

rules.title: Comparing decimal numbers with ==
patterns: ^floating-point comparison is always (?P<result>false|true); constant cannot be represented exactly in type '(?P<type>[^']+)'$
^comparing floating point with == or != is unsafe$
rules.what: On line {line} decimal numbers are compared with `==`. Decimal numbers are stored only approximately: a `float` holding 0.1 is really 0.100000001, while the constant `0.1` is a `double` 0.1000000000000000055 - so the two are NOT equal and `==` gives false.
why: Comparing a `float` with a `double` constant, or comparing results of decimal calculations exactly.
fix: Compare with a small tolerance: `fabs(x - 0.1) < 0.0001` (needs <math.h>).
Or make both sides the same type: `x == 0.1f`, or declare `x` as `double`.
samples: floating-point comparison is always false; constant cannot be represented exactly in type 'float'
